meta.title: Add Coral TPU to LXC | ProxMenux Documentation
meta.description: Pass a Google Coral TPU (USB or M.2 / PCIe) into a Proxmox LXC container. ProxMenux writes the right dev / cgroup / mount entries for each variant, boots the container, and installs the Edge TPU runtime inside so apps like Frigate can use the accelerator.

header.title: Add Coral TPU to LXC
header.description: Share a Google Coral TPU (USB Accelerator or M.2 / Mini-PCIe) with a Proxmox LXC container. ProxMenux handles the LXC config and the inside-container Edge TPU runtime install. Coral is TPU-only: for GPU / iGPU sharing (Quick Sync, VA-API, NVENC) in the same container, run Add GPU to LXC separately.

intro.title: What this does
intro.body: Writes the passthrough config into /etc/pve/lxc/<ctid>.conf — different entries depending on whether the host has a USB Accelerator, a M.2 / PCIe Coral, or both. Then it starts the container and installs Google's latest libedgetpu runtime inside it. iGPU / GPU passthrough is handled by a separate script (Add GPU to LXC) — this one focuses on the TPU.

whenUse.heading: When to use this
whenUse.body: Use this for <frigateLink>Frigate</frigateLink> or another compatible Linux detection app in LXC. Coral runs supported ML inference instead of the CPU. Performance depends on the model and hardware; video decoding and other application work still consume resources.

prereqs.title: Before you start
prereqs.drivers: Prepare the Coral device on the host. M.2 / PCIe needs the host driver loaded; USB needs device access and suitable permissions. See Install Coral TPU on the Host. The script installs the app runtime in Debian/Ubuntu containers; other distributions must provide it separately.
prereqs.container: An existing LXC container, ideally running a Debian / Ubuntu-based distro — the in-container runtime install uses apt-get. Non-Debian containers (Alpine, Arch, RHEL, SUSE…) are still supported in passthrough-only mode: the script detects the distro and offers a prompt to skip the libedgetpu APT install while still writing the device passthrough config — useful for app containers that bundle the runtime themselves (e.g. the Frigate Docker image).
prereqs.downtime: Be OK with a brief downtime of the container. The script stops it to apply config changes, then starts it back up to install drivers inside. No host reboot needed.

hostPrep.title: Host must be prepared first
hostPrep.body: M.2 / PCIe needs the host gasket/apex driver and a working device node. USB needs the connected device and permissions; it does not require the host to run the app. The libedgetpu runtime must be available where the app runs. Follow host preparation → LXC device access → app setup.

running.heading: Running the script
running.body: Open ProxMenux on the host, go to Hardware: GPUs and Coral-TPU → Add Coral TPU to LXC.
running.imageAlt: Menu entry for 'Add Coral TPU to LXC' inside Hardware: GPUs and Coral-TPU

howRuns.heading: How the script runs
howRuns.body: Choose the target container. The script configures USB access even if no USB Coral is currently connected, then adds M.2 / PCIe access when the corresponding hardware is detected.

pick.title: Pick the LXC container
pick.body: The picker lists eligible containers from pct list; OCI-image containers are hidden and managed through OCI manager Apps. Choose the target, running or stopped. The script stops it if needed, writes configuration and starts it for runtime installation.

gpuHint.title: GPU passthrough suggestion (optional)
gpuHint.body: If a GPU is detected but not configured for this container, a dialog recommends <lxcGpuLink>Add GPU to LXC</lxcGpuLink> for hardware video decoding, such as Quick Sync, VA-API or NVENC. It asks whether to continue with Coral only: Yes continues TPU setup; No exits so you can configure the GPU first.

usb.title: Write LXC config — USB path
usb.body: The script creates a host udev rule for the /dev/coral symlink and bind-mounts the whole /dev/bus/usb tree into the container. This USB configuration is written even when no Coral USB is currently connected; it exposes more than just that one device.
usb.whyBody: USB node paths such as /dev/bus/usb/001/005 change on reconnect. Older versions bind-mounted the /dev/coral symlink and could retain a stale path. Mounting the whole USB tree makes the current device node visible; the app may still need to reopen it.

pcie.title: Write LXC config — M.2 / PCIe path
pcie.body1: If a M.2 / PCIe Coral is present on the host and /dev/apex_0 exists (the apex kernel module is loaded), the script uses the modern Proxmox dev API which handles cgroup2 permissions automatically for both privileged and unprivileged containers:
pcie.body2: If /dev/apex_0 is absent after Install Coral on Host, the script writes a bind mount with create=file and, only when the apex major number is listed in /proc/devices, a classic cgroup2 rule. Neither creates a working device:
pcie.rebootTitle: Reboot the host first if you just installed Coral drivers
pcie.rebootBody: The fallback mount does not load the host apex driver. Load the driver, or reboot after installation, and verify the host device exists. Re-run the script once the device is ready to apply the modern device entry, then restart the container.

drivers.title: Start the container + install Coral runtime inside
drivers.body: The script starts the container and waits up to 15 seconds for its running status, then uses pct exec to run the runtime installer inside. The installer:
items: Imports Google's Coral GPG key to /etc/apt/keyrings/coral-edgetpu.gpg (modern path, same as the host installer uses) and adds the coral-edgetpu-stable APT repository with signed-by=.

Installs libedgetpu1-std by default. When an M.2 Coral is detected, the script offers a choice of libedgetpu1-std or libedgetpu1-max. The choice of runtime package does not itself configure application detection settings.
drivers.noIgpuBody: Earlier versions of this script also installed Intel va-driver-all, intel-opencl-icd and friends so the same container could do Quick Sync video decode alongside Coral inference. That doubled-up responsibility caused confusing failures when the user only wanted Coral. The iGPU side is now the exclusive job of Add GPU to LXC — run it first if you also want hardware video decode in the container.
drivers.debianBody: The in-container runtime install uses apt-get, which only ships on Debian/Ubuntu-family distros. On Alpine, Arch, RHEL or SUSE containers the script detects the distro via /etc/os-release and shows a confirmation prompt: continue in passthrough-only mode (writes the device config to /etc/pve/lxc/<ctid>.conf and skips the libedgetpu APT install) or abort. Passthrough-only is the right choice if the app container that will actually use Coral already bundles the runtime — the canonical example is the Frigate Docker image. Otherwise, follow Google's official guide to install libedgetpu manually after the script has written the LXC config.

summary.title: Summary
summary.body: The script prints a checklist at the end summarising what was enabled (Coral USB, Coral M.2) with ✓ or ⚠ marks depending on whether the hardware was actually detected. The container stays running — you can jump straight into Frigate / CodeProject.AI / your app config.

troubleshoot.heading: Troubleshooting
troubleshoot.apexBody: Check the host driver first: lsmod | grep apex. If missing, try modprobe apex or reboot after driver installation. Once /dev/apex_0 exists on the host, verify the LXC device entry (re-run the script if only the fallback entries were written) and restart the container with pct stop <ctid> && pct start <ctid>.
troubleshoot.replugTitle: USB Coral disappears after replug in a different port
troubleshoot.replugBody: This is exactly why the script mounts /dev/bus/usb instead of the /dev/coral symlink. If you're hitting this, check your LXC config has lxc.mount.entry: /dev/bus/usb dev/bus/usb ... and not a reference to /dev/coral directly. Old configs from earlier script versions may need updating — re-run the script on the same container and the config gets refreshed.
troubleshoot.alpineTitle: Alpine / Arch / RHEL / SUSE container — runtime not installed
troubleshoot.alpineBody: In passthrough-only mode, device configuration is written but libedgetpu is not installed. Use a compatible community package or build from source; check availability before using a package command such as Alpine apk add. An app image such as Frigate can bundle the runtime. With nested Docker, also forward the M.2 device using --device /dev/apex_0:/dev/apex_0, or mount the USB tree into that Docker container; the LXC mount alone does not forward it into Docker.
troubleshoot.frigateTitle: Frigate says 'Coral EdgeTPU detected but not available'
troubleshoot.frigateBody: Check runtime availability, device visibility and read/write access for the actual app process. For USB, inspect permissions and any plugdev membership. For M.2, inspect /dev/apex_0 with ls -l /dev/apex_0. A group name such as apex in /etc/group is not enough: numeric GIDs and LXC mappings must match. Also check whether another process already claims the TPU; do not switch to privileged mode as the first fix.
troubleshoot.logsTitle: Check both host and container logs
troubleshoot.logsBody: On the host, inspect kernel device messages with journalctl -k | grep -i -e apex -e gasket -e usb. Inside the container, inspect the app logs; for nested Docker use docker logs <container>. Permissions, missing runtime, USB connectivity or another process claiming the TPU can all cause failures.
